subject: Scam alert: the gift card that's empty on arrival
preheader: Check the package and the PIN strip before you pay, and keep the receipt.
html:
Check the package and the PIN strip before you pay, and keep the receipt.
Watch for this · Scam of the week · 2026-11-16

Gift cards drained before you even give them

Arrives by: store rack · From: a gift card that was tampered with on the shelf (fictional example)

The card on the rack looks normal, but the PIN strip has been peeled and re-covered, and the barcode has a sticker over it. You load $100. A week later it's empty.

3 tells

  1. A scratched, peeled or re-stuck PIN strip on the back.
  2. A torn or resealed package, or a second barcode sticker on top of the real one.
  3. The balance is gone before the person you gave it to ever used it.

Do this

  1. Check the package and the PIN area before you pay. Pick one from the back of the rack.
  2. Keep the receipt with the card, and give both together.
  3. Empty card? Call the brand on the card right away with the receipt, then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Already clicked, paid or shared? Card already drained? Contact the gift card company now, using the number on the back, and ask about a refund. Keep the receipt.

subject: Scam alert: the order you never placed
preheader: Don't call the number in the email. Check your orders in the store's own app.
html:
Don't call the number in the email. Check your orders in the store's own app.
Scam warning · Scam of the week · 2026-11-17

"Your $1,299 order is confirmed" emails with a number to call

Arrives by: email · From: a big online store or payment app (fictional example)

Order #A-77812 confirmed: MacBook Pro, $1,299.00. Not you? Call our fraud desk within 24 hours at 1-555-0142 to cancel and get a refund.

3 tells

  1. A big purchase you never made, sent to scare you into acting fast.
  2. A phone number to call, instead of "check your account".
  3. A deadline to cancel. On the call, they'll want remote access to your computer or your bank login "to refund you".

Do this

  1. Don't call the number in the email. Open the store's app or type its website yourself and check your orders.
  2. No order there? Delete the email. It's fake.
  3. Forward it to reportphishing@apwg.org and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Already clicked, paid or shared? Called and let them onto your computer? Disconnect it from the internet, call your bank on the number on your card, and change your passwords from another device.

subject: Scam alert: "send me the code to prove you're real"
preheader: A code someone sends you is a key to your account. Never read it back.
html:
A code someone sends you is a key to your account. Never read it back.
Scam warning · Scam of the week · 2026-11-18

Marketplace "buyers" who ask for a code to prove you're real

Arrives by: marketplace chat · From: a buyer for something you listed (fictional example)

Hi, is the stroller still available? Before I drive over, I want to make sure you're real. I'm sending you a code, just tell me what it says.

3 tells

  1. The buyer wants to "verify" you before they've even seen the item.
  2. A code arrives by text that you never asked for.
  3. They push you to read it back. That code lets them set up an account in your name or get into yours.

Do this

  1. Never share a code someone sends you, with anyone.
  2. Keep the chat inside the marketplace app, and sell in person, in a public place.
  3. Report the buyer in the app, then block them.

Already clicked, paid or shared? Read out a code? Change the password on your email and phone accounts now, turn on two-step sign-in, and ask your carrier to add a PIN.

subject: Scam alert: the call that sounds just like family
preheader: Voices can be copied. Hang up and call them back on the number you know.
html:
Voices can be copied. Hang up and call them back on the number you know.
Scam warning · Scam of the week · 2026-11-19

A family member's voice, crying for money

Arrives by: call · From: a grandchild, son or daughter, or someone "with" them (fictional example)

Grandma? It's me. I've been in an accident and I'm in trouble. Please don't tell Mom. A lawyer is going to call you, and I need $3,000 in gift cards today.

3 tells

  1. It's urgent and secret: don't tell anyone else in the family.
  2. A second person takes over: a "lawyer", "officer" or "bail agent".
  3. They want gift cards, cash, crypto or a wire. Those are hard to get back.

Do this

  1. Hang up and call the family member on the number you already have for them.
  2. Can't reach them? Call someone who's with them, or another relative.
  3. Agree on a family code word now, said out loud, never texted.

Already clicked, paid or shared? Sent money? Call the gift card company, bank or wire service right away and ask them to stop it. Then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

subject: Scam alert: the job that pays you to "rate products"
preheader: A job that makes you deposit money to unlock your pay is a scam.
html:
A job that makes you deposit money to unlock your pay is a scam.
Scam warning · Scam of the week · 2026-11-20

"Rate products from home, earn $800 a week" job texts

Arrives by: text or WhatsApp · From: a recruiter you never contacted (fictional example)

Hi! I'm Jenna, a recruiter. Part-time online work: rate products from home, 30 minutes a day, $800 a week. Reply YES to start. Small deposit to unlock higher-paying tasks.

3 tells

  1. A recruiter you never contacted texts out of the blue.
  2. Easy work for a lot of money, with no interview.
  3. You have to pay, often in crypto, to unlock tasks or withdraw what you "earned".

Do this

  1. Don't reply. Real employers don't recruit by surprise text and never ask you to pay to work.
  2. Look up the company yourself, and apply on its own careers page.
  3. Report the text: forward it to 7726 (SPAM), then delete it.

Already clicked, paid or shared? Paid in? Stop sending money; there's no withdrawal coming. Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and contact your bank or crypto exchange.

subject: Scam alert: the "package on hold" text
preheader: A $1.99 redelivery fee is how they get your card. Track packages in the shipper's app instead.
html:
A $1.99 redelivery fee is how they get your card. Track packages in the shipper's app instead.
Scam warning · Scam of the week · 2026-11-24

"Your package is on hold" texts are spiking before Black Friday

Arrives by: text · From: a delivery company, from a number you don't know (fictional example)

USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Update within 12 hours and pay a $1.99 redelivery fee: usps-redeliver-help.com

3 tells

  1. A text you didn't sign up for, from a regular phone number, about a package you can't name.
  2. A tiny fee and a short deadline. The fee is the bait; the page wants your full card details.
  3. A link that only looks like the shipper's site. The real domain is right before the first single slash.

Do this

  1. Don't tap. Track packages in the shipper's app or by typing its website yourself.
  2. Expecting something? Check the order page on the store's own site or app.
  3. Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM), then delete it.

Already clicked, paid or shared? Typed your card number? Call the number on the back of your card and ask for a new one. Then watch your statement for small test charges.
